agent_notes: אֱלֹהִים is plural in form and has no article. Rashi reads it as angels/princes, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David as judges and the wise (as in Ex 22:8), the Targum as 'judges'. The five English versions all say 'the gods'. I kept 'gods' in the literal layer and in the dramatic layer, and set out the readings in the commentary rather than choosing one.
The superscription 'of David' is KJV verse 0 and the Hebrew verse 1. The LXX adds a reference to Haggai and Zechariah; I do not mention it because it is not in the packet.

'Over all your name your word' (עַל־כָּל־שִׁמְךָ אִמְרָתֶךָ) is syntactically ambiguous. KJV/ASV read 'you have magnified your word above all your name'. Radak and Meiri read the nouns as reversed ('your name above all your word'), and Ibn Ezra and Rashi each take 'name' as the divine attributes. I kept the Hebrew word order in the literal layer and followed the KJV reading in the dramatic layer, flagging the ambiguity in the commentary.

agent_notes: יְיֵדָע is an unusual form. The commentaries (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Meiri, Metzudat David and Zion) read it as a causative of ידע, 'he makes known / disciplines', citing Judg 8:16 (וַיּוֹדַע); Radak takes it as 'he makes known'. I glossed and translated it as the plain 'he knows' that the five versions share and put the other reading in the commentary. The claim that 'knows from afar' means 'keeps at a distance' is a common reading, not one I can source to a lexicon.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses יִגְמֹר as 'he will avenge'. I corrected it to 'he will complete': גמר means to bring to an end, to finish, and 'avenge' does not fit בַּעֲדִי ('on my behalf'). The Targum has 'will complete evil upon them', which does read it as vengeance; I note this in the commentary. In the Hebrew the second יהוה is a vocative at the head of the next clause, as the accents show.
Malbim's gloss on אַל־תֶּרֶף ('as a father does not let go of his son') is paraphrased from the packet and not quoted.
